source.title: An Investigation of Why Overparameterization Exacerbates Spurious Correlations
source.authors: Shiori Sagawa; Aditi Raghunathan; Pang Wei Koh; Percy Liang

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model size and measures test error, but its central question and principal outcome are worst-group error under spurious correlations rather than the original average-error double-descent curve.
record.gate_note: The paper reports size-sweep outcomes for average and worst-group test error. It also reports regularization and subsampling results, but these do not test whether the peak in the claim appears over epochs, sample size, or a unified effective-complexity axis. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps ResNet10 width on CelebA and random-feature count on Waterbirds and synthetic data, past zero training error. It reports that average test error keeps improving there, which bears on the second descent in V1 and V4. Its main outcome, worst-group error under spurious correlations, is a different construct (minority-group error under distribution shift). It is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that overparameterization improves average test error but hurts worst-group error under spurious correlations. They attribute the harm to group imbalance, informative spurious features, and an inductive bias toward memorizing fewer points. Subsampling the majority group restores low worst-group error for overparameterized models.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies network width or random-feature count and evaluates test error, as in capacity-scaling work, but emphasizes worst-group error on spurious-correlation datasets rather than reproducing the original average-error double-descent setting.
record.method_sensitivity: Worst-group outcomes depend on group balance, the relative informativeness of spurious and core features, training objective, regularization strength, and whether the data are subsampled. The paper also notes that worst-group error can be unstable across epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the reweighted objective on full data, worst-group test error worsens as model size grows past zero training error: CelebA 25.6% to >60%, Waterbirds 26.6% to ≥42.4%, synthetic 28.5% to ~55%. Meanwhile average error improves. The harm vanishes when the spurious feature is removed, with balanced groups (pmaj=0.5), or with majority subsampling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterization past interpolation can hurt worst-group (minority) test error under spurious correlations even while average test error improves. The effect depends on group imbalance and the informativeness of spurious features.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The relevant capacity trends are largely described qualitatively or shown in figures; uncertainty intervals are not stated. The paper reports that worst-group error can be unstable across epochs because of small sample size and relatively large learning rate, and averages reported results over the last 10 epochs.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows left out.

untested.parts: Whether test error rises and peaks near the size that just fits the training set. Only the final descent is reported.
No test error over epochs is reported. Errors are averaged over the last 10 epochs.
No sweep of sample size near the interpolation threshold. Subsampling also changes group balance.
The classical U-shaped part and the peak at interpolation for random-feature models.
Not tested. The regularization sweeps concern worst-group error and the absence of zero training error, not a double-descent peak.

missing.what: ERM-trained average test error improves past zero training error: best 4.6% at CelebA width 96, 4.2% at 6,000 Waterbirds features, 9.0% at 9,000 synthetic features.
Average test error improves with overparameterization for all pmaj and SCR settings on synthetic data.
Average error under subsampling: overparameterized CelebA model reaches 11.1% average test error, and overparameterization helps average error across all three datasets.
Strong L2 regularization hurts average error in overparameterized models; best average error comes with near-zero regularization.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'challenges' label (r4–r6) and 'limits_scope' label (r7–r8) are removed because worst-group error is not the risk V4 names; these findings now sit under fits_no_version. The reader's V1 'limits_scope' label is replaced by 'supports' restricted to the second descent, with the peak listed as untested. Figures cannot be read from the text, so whether any average-error peak appears in Figures 3 and 4 is undetermined. The datasets carry no added label noise, which may explain why no peak is discussed.

versions.untested_parts: The average-error size sweep is reported, but the text does not establish a fall-rise-fall curve or locate a peak near the point of zero training error.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
The study does not sweep training-set size near an interpolation threshold. Its subsampling experiments change group balance and training procedure as well as the amount of data.
The study reports capacity-related average and worst-group error trends, but does not establish a complete classical U-shaped-to-second-descent curve for each model class.
The paper proposes a memorization-based explanation but does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The paper studies regularization and the relative informativeness of core and spurious features, but does not test whether label noise drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes that peak.
The study does not measure error against an effective number of parameters or test whether that reparameterization turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
